compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional apartment building outage, one staff member checks in with the site lead while another drafts a message. Either type can do either task. Who has the information or is authorized to publish matters more than the four letters.

The two codes have no letters in common, yet both stacks contain Se, Ti, Fe, and Ni in the notation used here. Distance, duty, and access to information can make people with different preferences do the same work.

Separate four questions: where attention and energy tend to go (E/I), what information carries weight (S/N), what criteria guide a decision (T/F), and how someone approaches outward commitments or open options (J/P). Job requirements often explain a single action.

### One repair bulletin, two notices that solve different problems

In this fictional outage, a water main breaks and three buildings lose water. Two staff members have the same authority and bulletin: the crew is due at eight, the restoration time is unknown, and the confirmed water pickup point is at the east gate.

One way to read the bulletin is to check which locations and times it confirms. Another is to connect those details and ask whether some buildings may miss a pickup update. Either person can check facts and consider possible implications.

A notice that gives only locations and times may leave people unsure how to ask for help. A message focused on reassurance may leave them unsure what is already in place. Staff can include confirmed facts and label any estimates they are authorized to share.

In this fictional building, a notice template can distinguish confirmed facts, estimates, and the next update. Staff can agree who verifies and publishes each update. This checks communication, not type.

### Why the same four parts come out in reverse order

In type dynamics, ESTP’s P points to its outward-facing perceiving process. With E, that process is dominant extraverted Sensing (Se), paired with auxiliary introverted Thinking (Ti). INFJ’s J points to its outward-facing judging process. With I, that process is auxiliary extraverted Feeling (Fe), paired with dominant introverted Intuition (Ni).

In the convention used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se. Se and Ni switch the dominant and inferior positions, while Ti and Fe switch the auxiliary and tertiary positions. The order describes the model and does not indicate what someone does first or does well.

An INFJ can relay a verified update, and an ESTP can make sure a notice includes a way to ask for help. Either can do both. Neither the action nor someone’s response afterward establishes a function order.

The Foundation lists tertiary Feeling for ESTP (Fe or Fi) and tertiary Thinking for INFJ (Te or Ti). This page uses Fe and Ti, so the exact four-position reversal applies to this convention. Read more in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

compare_blocks.body:
All six rows use the same fictional outage, bulletin, residents, deadline, and publication authority.

Either person can weigh both considerations in each row. The final row illustrates complementary tasks that do not distinguish the types.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional apartment building outage, one staff member checks in with the site lead while another drafts a message. Either type can do either task. Who has the information or is authorized to publish matters more than the four letters.

The two codes have no letters in common, yet both stacks contain Se, Ti, Fe, and Ni in the notation used here. Distance, duty, and access to information can make people with different preferences do the same work.

Separate four questions: where attention and energy tend to go (E/I), what information carries weight (S/N), what criteria guide a decision (T/F), and how someone approaches outward commitments or open options (J/P). Job requirements often explain a single action.

### One repair bulletin, two notices that solve different problems

In this fictional outage, a water main breaks and three buildings lose water. Two staff members have the same authority and bulletin: the crew is due at eight, the restoration time is unknown, and the confirmed water pickup point is at the east gate.

One way to read the bulletin is to check which locations and times it confirms. Another is to connect those details and ask whether some buildings may miss a pickup update. Either person can check facts and consider possible implications.

A notice that gives only locations and times may leave people unsure how to ask for help. A message focused on reassurance may leave them unsure what is already in place. Staff can include confirmed facts and label any estimates they are authorized to share.

In this fictional building, a notice template can distinguish confirmed facts, estimates, and the next update. Staff can agree who verifies and publishes each update. This checks communication, not type.

### Why the same four parts come out in reverse order

In type dynamics, ESTP’s P points to its outward-facing perceiving process. With E, that process is dominant extraverted Sensing (Se), paired with auxiliary introverted Thinking (Ti). INFJ’s J points to its outward-facing judging process. With I, that process is auxiliary extraverted Feeling (Fe), paired with dominant introverted Intuition (Ni).

In the convention used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se. Se and Ni switch the dominant and inferior positions, while Ti and Fe switch the auxiliary and tertiary positions. The order describes the model and does not indicate what someone does first or does well.

An INFJ can relay a verified update, and an ESTP can make sure a notice includes a way to ask for help. Either can do both. Neither the action nor someone’s response afterward establishes a function order.

The Foundation lists tertiary Feeling for ESTP (Fe or Fi) and tertiary Thinking for INFJ (Te or Ti). This page uses Fe and Ti, so the exact four-position reversal applies to this convention. Read more in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

compare_blocks.body:
Both examples are fictional. The building staff’s role is to share verified information. The site lead and qualified crew are responsible for outage response and repairs.

One notice can do two jobs: explain what has been confirmed and tell residents where to ask questions. Either person can verify facts or review the wording, depending on their access and authority.

### ESTP and INFJ: three buildings dry, who writes and who tracks

In this fictional outage, the two people on duty need to send one consistent update. Two notices could give residents conflicting information.

Use the authorized communications process. Confirm the facts with the site lead and have the authorized person publish the update. Either type can prepare the wording, including how to ask for help and when to expect another update, if known.

### ESTP and INFJ: a friend is misread in the group chat

In this fictional group chat, someone suggests a friend still owes money. A response could correct a verified factual error or address how a public reply would affect the friend. Either person can consider both. Access to a private record does not grant permission to share it.

A quick correction may clarify the claim, but it can also draw more attention to private details. Checking with the friend gives them a say in how to respond. Either person can weigh those concerns.

Ask the friend whether they want a reply, who should give it, and what details they agree to share. Keep transfer records private unless they give permission. Silence is not consent, and either type can respect that boundary.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional apartment building outage, one staff member checks in with the site lead while another drafts a message. Either type can do either task. Who has the information or is authorized to publish matters more than the four letters.

The two codes have no letters in common, yet both stacks contain Se, Ti, Fe, and Ni in the notation used here. Distance, duty, and access to information can make people with different preferences do the same work.

Separate four questions: where attention and energy tend to go (E/I), what information carries weight (S/N), what criteria guide a decision (T/F), and how someone approaches outward commitments or open options (J/P). Job requirements often explain a single action.

### One repair bulletin, two notices that solve different problems

In this fictional outage, a water main breaks and three buildings lose water. Two staff members have the same authority and bulletin: the crew is due at eight, the restoration time is unknown, and the confirmed water pickup point is at the east gate.

One way to read the bulletin is to check which locations and times it confirms. Another is to connect those details and ask whether some buildings may miss a pickup update. Either person can check facts and consider possible implications.

A notice that gives only locations and times may leave people unsure how to ask for help. A message focused on reassurance may leave them unsure what is already in place. Staff can include confirmed facts and label any estimates they are authorized to share.

In this fictional building, a notice template can distinguish confirmed facts, estimates, and the next update. Staff can agree who verifies and publishes each update. This checks communication, not type.

### Why the same four parts come out in reverse order

In type dynamics, ESTP’s P points to its outward-facing perceiving process. With E, that process is dominant extraverted Sensing (Se), paired with auxiliary introverted Thinking (Ti). INFJ’s J points to its outward-facing judging process. With I, that process is auxiliary extraverted Feeling (Fe), paired with dominant introverted Intuition (Ni).

In the convention used here, ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se. Se and Ni switch the dominant and inferior positions, while Ti and Fe switch the auxiliary and tertiary positions. The order describes the model and does not indicate what someone does first or does well.

An INFJ can relay a verified update, and an ESTP can make sure a notice includes a way to ask for help. Either can do both. Neither the action nor someone’s response afterward establishes a function order.

The Foundation lists tertiary Feeling for ESTP (Fe or Fi) and tertiary Thinking for INFJ (Te or Ti). This page uses Fe and Ti, so the exact four-position reversal applies to this convention. Read more in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

All six rows use the same fictional outage, bulletin, residents, deadline, and publication authority.

Either person can weigh both considerations in each row. The final row illustrates complementary tasks that do not distinguish the types.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deciding which details to verify or explore | Which buildings, arrival time, and pickup location the bulletin confirms | What the affected buildings and pickup location together suggest about possible gaps in coverage | S/N: confirmed details and potential implications. Either person can consider both. |
| Planning the next update while restoration is uncertain | Keep feasible update times open while the same estimate is uncertain | Set a provisional update time while making the same uncertainty clear | J/P: keeping options open or setting a provisional arrangement. Either can revise the plan. |

| Reviewing the same resident feedback | Attention may turn outward toward the exchange as staff make sense of the feedback | Attention may turn inward toward reflecting on the same feedback | E/I: orientation of attention and energy. Neither implies who speaks first. |

An experienced INFJ and an experienced ESTP can give the same update when the information and responsibilities match. The table illustrates preferences without measuring skill or establishing a type.
sections.title: ESTP and INFJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Both examples are fictional. The building staff’s role is to share verified information. The site lead and qualified crew are responsible for outage response and repairs.

One notice can do two jobs: explain what has been confirmed and tell residents where to ask questions. Either person can verify facts or review the wording, depending on their access and authority.

### ESTP and INFJ: three buildings dry, who writes and who tracks

In this fictional outage, the two people on duty need to send one consistent update. Two notices could give residents conflicting information.

Use the authorized communications process. Confirm the facts with the site lead and have the authorized person publish the update. Either type can prepare the wording, including how to ask for help and when to expect another update, if known.

### ESTP and INFJ: a friend is misread in the group chat

In this fictional group chat, someone suggests a friend still owes money. A response could correct a verified factual error or address how a public reply would affect the friend. Either person can consider both. Access to a private record does not grant permission to share it.

A quick correction may clarify the claim, but it can also draw more attention to private details. Checking with the friend gives them a say in how to respond. Either person can weigh those concerns.

Ask the friend whether they want a reply, who should give it, and what details they agree to share. Keep transfer records private unless they give permission. Silence is not consent, and either type can respect that boundary.

A direct update can reflect access to confirmed information. It tells you little about someone’s willingness to take risks.

Leaving a time out can be the accurate choice when no reliable estimate is available. That tells you little about someone’s ability to make decisions.

Distance, assigned duties, and access to information can explain who reaches the site or posts the first message. Timing cannot establish the person’s preferences.

Different letters do not make two people opposites in every respect. The types share process names in the notation used here and can reach the same conclusions.

items.answer:
Sensing emphasizes what can be verified now, such as which buildings lost water. Intuition emphasizes connections and possibilities, such as whether the location of a pickup point could leave gaps in access.

Either person can notice both. Position, experience, and authority can affect which information they have or need. A single episode cannot establish S/N.
items.question: What might ESTP and INFJ notice in the same situation?

items.answer:
In the notation used here, ESTP’s dominant Se and auxiliary Ti appear in INFJ’s fourth and third positions. INFJ’s dominant Ni and auxiliary Fe appear in ESTP’s fourth and third positions.

The full reversal depends on the notation for the tertiary process. The stack describes a theoretical arrangement. It cannot predict speed, ability, or whether two people will get along.
items.question: Why are the ESTP and INFJ function stacks reversed?

items.answer:

items.question: Can an INFJ give a direct update and an ESTP write a detailed notice?

items.answer:
Use the site’s authorized communications process. The person with access to confirmed information verifies it with the site lead. The authorized staff member publishes the update.

Either type can write or review the update when assigned. The notice should make it easy to see what is confirmed, what is still uncertain, and where residents can get a verified update.
items.question: Who should write the first update in the fictional outage?

items.answer:
Either friend might want to correct a claim right away or take time to decide whether to reply. That choice depends on the people involved, what is known, and what can be shared.

Ask the person involved whether they want a reply and what details may be shared. That agreement protects their privacy regardless of anyone’s type.
